claim: voyAGEr is a free web interface for the analysis of age-related gene expression alterations in human tissues.
source: We herein introduce voyAGEr, an online graphical interface to explore age-related gene expression alterations in 49 human tissues.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the purpose and nature of voyAGEr.

claim: voyAGEr analyzes gene expression alterations in 49 human tissues.
source: We herein introduce voyAGEr, an online graphical interface to explore age-related gene expression alterations in 49 human tissues.
evidence: The manuscript states the number of tissues analyzed.

claim: voyAGEr's development involved a novel bioinformatics pipeline leveraging RNA sequencing data from the GTEx project.
source: In its conception, we developed a novel bioinformatics pipeline leveraging RNA sequencing data, from the GTEx project, encompassing more than 900 individuals.
evidence: The abstract describes the data source and pipeline development.

claim: The GTEx data used in voyAGEr encompasses more than 900 individuals.
source: In its conception, we developed a novel bioinformatics pipeline leveraging RNA sequencing data, from the GTEx project, encompassing more than 900 individuals.
evidence: The abstract specifies the sample size.

claim: voyAGEr reveals transcriptomic signatures of asynchronous ageing between tissues.
source: voyAGEr reveals transcriptomic signatures of the known asynchronous ageing between tissues, allowing the observation of tissue-specific age periods of major transcriptional changes, associated with alterations in different biological pathways, cellular composition, and disease conditions.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the tool.

claim: voyAGEr allows observation of tissue-specific age periods of major transcriptional changes.
source: voyAGEr reveals transcriptomic signatures of the known asynchronous ageing between tissues, allowing the observation of tissue-specific age periods of major transcriptional changes, associated with alterations in different biological pathways, cellular composition, and disease conditions.
evidence: The abstract describes this capability of the tool.

claim: voyAGEr was created to assist researchers with no expertise in bioinformatics.
source: Notably, voyAGEr was created to assist researchers with no expertise in bioinformatics, providing a supportive framework for elaborating, testing and refining their hypotheses on the molecular nature of human ageing and its association with pathologies, thereby also aiding in the discovery of novel therapeutic targets.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the target user group.

claim: voyAGEr is freely available at https://compbio.imm.medicina.ulisboa.pt/app/voyAGEr.
source: voyAGEr is freely available at https://compbio.imm.medicina.ulisboa.pt/app/voyAGEr.
evidence: The abstract and manuscript provide the URL.

claim: Age is a prevalent risk factor for many human pathologies, including cancer, neurodegenerative, and cardiovascular diseases.
source: The ageing-associated progressive loss of proper tissue homeostasis maintenance makes age a prevalent risk factor for many human pathologies, including cancer, neurodegenerative, and cardiovascular diseases (Campisi, 2013; Niccoli and Partridge, 2012; Wyss-Coray, 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature supporting this claim.

claim: Dynamic transcriptional alterations accompany most physiological processes occurring in human tissues.
source: Dynamic transcriptional alterations accompany most physiological processes occurring in human tissues (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature supporting this claim.

claim: A small proportion of transcripts has been shown to vary with age in tissue.
source: A small proportion of transcripts has indeed been shown to vary with age in tissue (Stegeman and Weake, 2017) and sex-specific (Tower, 2017; Austad and Fischer, 2016; Melé et al., 2015; Gershoni and Pietrokovski, 2017; Kassam et al., 2019; Mayne et al., 2016) manners.
evidence: The introduction cites published literature supporting this claim.

claim: Transcript variation with age occurs in sex-specific manners.
source: A small proportion of transcripts has indeed been shown to vary with age in tissue (Stegeman and Weake, 2017) and sex-specific (Tower, 2017; Austad and Fischer, 2016; Melé et al., 2015; Gershoni and Pietrokovski, 2017; Kassam et al., 2019; Mayne et al., 2016) manners.
evidence: The introduction cites multiple published studies supporting this claim.

claim: Age-related variations in transcripts reflect dysregulations of gene expression that underlie cellular dysfunctions.
source: Such variations reflect dysregulations of gene expression that underlie cellular dysfunctions (Stegeman and Weake, 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature supporting this claim.

claim: Many studies analysed age-related changes in gene expression in rodent tissues.
source: Many studies analysed the age-related changes in gene expression in rodent tissues (Zahn et al., 2007; Kimmel et al., 2019; Benayoun et al., 2019; Lui et al., 2010; Shavlakadze et al., 2019; Almanzar et al., 2020; Schaum et al., 2020), emphasising the role in ageing of genes related to inflammatory responses, cell cycle, or the electron transport chain.
evidence: The introduction cites multiple published studies.

claim: Rodent studies emphasise the role in ageing of genes related to inflammatory responses, cell cycle, or the electron transport chain.
source: Many studies analysed the age-related changes in gene expression in rodent tissues (Zahn et al., 2007; Kimmel et al., 2019; Benayoun et al., 2019; Lui et al., 2010; Shavlakadze et al., 2019; Almanzar et al., 2020; Schaum et al., 2020), emphasising the role in ageing of genes related to inflammatory responses, cell cycle, or the electron transport chain.
evidence: The introduction summarizes findings from cited rodent studies.

claim: Most studies on human tissues focused on a single tissue.
source: Indeed, most studies aimed at profiling ageing-related gene expression changes in human tissues focused on a single tissue (e.g. muscle Zahn et al., 2005; Welle et al., 2003; Jozsi et al., 2000, kidney Rodwell et al., 2004, brain Galatro et al., 2017; Olah et al., 2018; Berchtold et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2004; Işıldak et al., 2020, skin Haustead et al., 2016; Holzscheck et al., 2020, blood Nakamura et al., 2012; Harries et al., 2011, liver Thomas et al., 2002, retina Yoshida et al., 2002) and/or are limited to a comparison between young and old individuals (Welle et al., 2003; Jozsi et al., 2000; Haustead et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2002), failing to fully capture the changes of the tissue-specific gene expression landscape throughout ageing (Stegeman and Weake, 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies and characterizes their scope.

claim: A few studies were led on more than one tissue in humans, from post-mortem samples and biopsies.
source: A few studies were nonetheless led on more than one tissue in humans, from post-mortem samples (Gheorghe et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015) and biopsies (Aramillo Irizar et al., 2018; Glass et al., 2013), and in mice (Schaum et al., 2020; Aramillo Irizar et al., 2018) and rats (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites published multi-tissue studies.

claim: Multi-tissue studies highlight an asynchronous ageing of tissues.
source: The age-related transcriptional profiles derived therein, either from regression (Schaum et al., 2020; Gheorghe et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015; Glass et al., 2013) or comparison between age groups (Aramillo Irizar et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2014), highlight an asynchronous ageing of tissues (discussed in Rando and Wyss-Coray, 2021), with some of them more affected by age-related gene expression changes associated with biological mechanisms known to be impacted by ageing such as mitochondrial activity or metabolic homeostasis.
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies supporting this finding.

claim: Tissue-specific periods of major transcriptional changes in the fifth and eighth decades of the human lifespan have been revealed.
source: In particular, tissue-specific periods of major transcriptional changes in the fifth and eighth decades of the human lifespan have been revealed (Gheorghe et al., 2014), reflecting the so-called digital ageing (Rando and Wyss-Coray, 2021), consistent with what is observed in mice (Almanzar et al., 2020; Schaum et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites published studies supporting this claim.

claim: Some synchronisation was found between tissues like the lung, heart, and whole blood, which exhibit a co-ageing pattern.
source: Furthermore, despite outlining the tissue specificity of the transcriptomic signatures of human ageing, some synchronisation was found between tissues like the lung, heart, and whole blood, which exhibit a co-ageing pattern (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a published study supporting this claim.

claim: Processed data from previous studies have not been made easily accessible and interpretable to researchers lacking computational proficiency.
source: Processed data from those studies have not been made easily accessible and interpretable to researchers lacking computational proficiency but aiming to use them to test their novel hypotheses.
evidence: The introduction identifies a gap in the field that voyAGEr addresses.

claim: voyAGEr provides flexible visualisation of comprehensive functional analyses of gene expression alterations occurring in 49 human tissues with age in each biological sex.
source: To fill this void, we have developed voyAGEr, a web application providing flexible visualisation of comprehensive functional analyses of gene expression alterations occurring in 49 human tissues with age in each biological sex.
evidence: The introduction describes the capabilities of voyAGEr.

claim: voyAGEr leverages the large RNA-seq dataset from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project.
source: We leverage the large RNA-seq dataset from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project (Lonsdale et al., 2013), encompassing tissue samples from hundreds of donors aged from 20 to 70 years, with a pipeline for gene expression profiling with an optimised temporal resolution.
evidence: The introduction cites the data source.

claim: The GTEx dataset encompasses tissue samples from hundreds of donors aged from 20 to 70 years.
source: We leverage the large RNA-seq dataset from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project (Lonsdale et al., 2013), encompassing tissue samples from hundreds of donors aged from 20 to 70 years, with a pipeline for gene expression profiling with an optimised temporal resolution.
evidence: The introduction describes the dataset characteristics.

claim: voyAGEr allows investigation of ageing from a gene-centric perspective.
source: voyAGEr allows us to investigate ageing from two perspectives: (i) gene-centric – how each gene's tissue-specific expression progresses with age; and (ii) tissue-centric – how tissue-specific transcriptomes change with age.
evidence: The introduction describes the analytical perspectives offered by voyAGEr.

claim: voyAGEr allows investigation of ageing from a tissue-centric perspective.
source: voyAGEr allows us to investigate ageing from two perspectives: (i) gene-centric – how each gene's tissue-specific expression progresses with age; and (ii) tissue-centric – how tissue-specific transcriptomes change with age.
evidence: The introduction describes the analytical perspectives offered by voyAGEr.

claim: voyAGEr enables examination of modules of co-expressed genes altered with age in four tissues: brain cortex, skeletal muscle, left ventricle of the heart, and whole blood.
source: Additionally, voyAGEr enables the examination of modules of co-expressed genes altered with age in four tissues (brain cortex, skeletal muscle, left ventricle of the heart, whole blood), namely their enrichment in specific cell types, biological pathways, and association with diseases.
evidence: The introduction describes this specific functionality.

claim: voyAGEr is open-source.
source: Moreover, being open-source, voyAGEr can be adapted by fellow developers to be used with alternative datasets (e.g. from other species) or to incorporate other specific functionalities.
evidence: The introduction states the open-source nature of the tool.

claim: The ShARP-LM approach consists of performing differential gene expression in moving age windows spanning 16 years.
source: We named our approach Shifting Age Range Pipeline for Linear Modelling (ShARP-LM). Briefly, this method consists of performing differential gene expression (with gene expression as a function of the donors' Age, Sex, and Age&Sex interaction) in moving age windows spanning 16 years.
evidence: The Results section describes the ShARP-LM methodology.

claim: ShARP-LM uses a sliding window with window size = 16 and step size = 1 years of age.
source: For each tissue, we fitted linear models to the gene expression of samples from donors with ages within windows with a range of 16 years shifted through consecutive years of age (i.e. in a sliding window with window size = 16 and step size = 1 years of age).
evidence: The Methods section specifies the window parameters.

claim: 16 years was the minimum age span needed to guarantee the presence of more than one sample per window across all considered tissues.
source: This was the minimum age span needed to guarantee the presence of more than one sample per window, across all considered tissues.
evidence: The Methods section explains the rationale for the window size.

claim: The window size gradually increases from 11 to 16 years when starting from the 'youngest' samples and decreases from 16 to 11 years when reaching the 'oldest.'
source: As samples at the ends of the dataset's age range would be thereby involved in fewer linear models, we made the window size gradually increase from 11 to 16 years when starting from the 'youngest' samples and decrease from 16 to 11 years when reaching the 'oldest' (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Methods section describes this adjustment and references a figure.

claim: Major age-related transcriptional alterations in coronary artery are found at around 60 years of age.
source: For example, in coronary artery: major age-related transcriptional alterations are found at around 60 years of age (upper left panel), illustrated by the behaviour of COX11 (bottom left panel)
evidence: Figure 1 caption describes this finding with reference to the figure panels.

claim: Major gene expression differences between males and females in coronary artery happen across the considered age range.
source: major gene expression differences between males and females happen across the considered age range (upper centre panel), as illustrated by CD99 (bottom centre panel)
evidence: Figure 1 caption describes this finding with reference to the figure panels.

claim: Major differences between sexes in age-related gene expression alterations in coronary artery happen across the considered age range.
source: major differences between sexes in age-related gene expression alterations happen across the considered age range (upper right panel), as illustrated by AKT2 (bottom right panel)
evidence: Figure 1 caption describes this finding with reference to the figure panels.

claim: Tissue accounts for approximately 90% of the total variance in the dataset.
source: (Left panel) Tissue accounts for approximately 90% of the total variance, while donor contributes around 10%; age has a minimal impact (1%), likely due to the relative subtlety of its effects on gene expression and to the tissue specificity of ageing dynamics.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B caption describes variance analysis results.

claim: Donor contributes around 10% to the total variance in the dataset.
source: (Left panel) Tissue accounts for approximately 90% of the total variance, while donor contributes around 10%; age has a minimal impact (1%), likely due to the relative subtlety of its effects on gene expression and to the tissue specificity of ageing dynamics.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B caption describes variance analysis results.

claim: Age has a minimal impact (1%) on the total variance in the dataset.
source: (Left panel) Tissue accounts for approximately 90% of the total variance, while donor contributes around 10%; age has a minimal impact (1%), likely due to the relative subtlety of its effects on gene expression and to the tissue specificity of ageing dynamics.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B caption describes variance analysis results.

claim: Removal of the donor variable does not transfer variance to age, suggesting limited confounding between the two variables.
source: (Right panel) Removal of the donor variable does not transfer variance to age, suggesting limited confounding between the two variables.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B caption describes variance analysis results.

claim: Before batch effect correction, 17.7% of the variance between samples appears to be mainly explained by the COHORT variable.
source: (Top) Before batch effect correction, 17.7% of the variance between samples appears to be mainly explained by the COHORT variable.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption describes batch effect analysis.

claim: After batch effect correction, PC1 no longer appears to be explained by the COHORT variable.
source: (Bottom) After batch effect correction, PC1 no longer appears to be explained by the COHORT variable, with its weights having a similar distribution between batches.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption describes batch effect correction results.

claim: CDKN2A has its expression increased with age in the vast majority of tissues profiled.
source: CDKN2A, that encodes cell cycle regulatory protein p16INK4A known to accumulate in senescent cells Gil and Peters, 2006; Erickson et al., 1998), has its expression increased with age in the vast majority of tissues profiled (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A ).
evidence: The Results section describes this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: PCNA and MKI67 have their expression altered with age in the lung.
source: These genes have their expression altered with age in the lung and display a similar expression profile (decreasing from 25 to 30 years old, constant between 35 and 50 years old and decreasing in older ages) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The Results section describes this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Sex biases have been reported in the expression of SALL1 and DDX43 in adipose tissue and lung, respectively.
source: On a different note, sex biases have been reported in the expression of SALL1 and DDX43 in adipose tissue and lung, respectively (Kassam et al., 2019).
evidence: The Results section cites a published study.

claim: voyAGEr allows assessment of the temporal window where sex biases in gene expression occur.
source: voyAGEr allows us to not only recapitulate those observations but also assess the temporal window where these changes occur (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section describes this capability with reference to a figure.

claim: A heatmap displaying the statistical significance over age of the proportion of genes altered with Age, Sex, or Age&Sex illustrates the asynchronous ageing of tissues.
source: A heatmap displaying, for all tissues, the statistical significance over age (v. Methods) of the proportion of genes altered with Age, Sex, or Age&Sex (depending on the user's interest) is initially shown (Figure 3A), illustrating the aforementioned asynchronous ageing of tissues observed for humans and rodents (Schaum et al., 2020; Thomas et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2002; Gheorghe et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015; Aramillo Irizar et al., 2018; Rando and Wyss-Coray, 2021).
evidence: The Results section describes this visualization with citations.

claim: voyAGEr enables the identification of a prominent age period of transcriptional alterations in the uterus, which coincides with the onset of menopause.
source: voyAGEr enables the identification of a prominent age period of transcriptional alterations in the uterus, which coincides with the onset of menopause (Kaczmarek, 2014).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 caption describes this finding with a citation.

claim: The subcutaneous adipose tissue appears to go through two main periods of transcriptional changes with age: a major one at the late 20s (~13% of altered genes), and a minor one after 45 years (~5% of altered genes).
source: As an example, the subcutaneous adipose tissue appears to go through two main periods of transcriptional changes with age: a major one at the late 20s (~13% of altered genes), and a minor one after 45 years (~5% of altered genes) (Figure 3B, A).
evidence: The Results section describes this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Mammary is the tissue with the most sex-differentiated gene expression.
source: Mammary is corroborated as the tissue with the most sex-differentiated gene expression.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2A caption describes this finding.

claim: For tissues like Adipose - Subcutaneous, Skin - Not Sun Exposed, Thyroid, Nerve - Tibial, Muscle - Skeletal, and Spleen, sex-related biases in expression mainly arise in late life.
source: For tissues like Adipose - Subcutaneous, Skin - Not Sun Exposed, Thyroid, Nerve - Tibial, Muscle - Skeletal, and Spleen, sex-related biases in expression mainly arise in late life.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2A caption describes this finding.

claim: The statistical power for detecting transcriptional changes is influenced by the age distribution of donors.
source: The statistical power for detecting transcriptional changes is influenced by the age distribution of donors, leading to a higher likelihood of identifying significant alterations (FDR ≤ 0.05) in age ranges that are more prevalent in the sample population, typically associated with older individuals.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 3 caption describes this limitation.

claim: voyAGEr performs Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) using the Reactome database.
source: voyAGEr performs Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) and the user can visualise heatmaps displaying the evolution over the age of the resulting normalised enrichment score (NES Subramanian et al., 2005, reflecting the degree to which a pathway is over- or under-represented in a subset of genes) for a given tissue, effect (Age, Sex, or Age&Sex) and Reactome pathway (all, or user-selected) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The Results section describes this functionality with citations.

claim: Pathways were clustered into families that include Reactome, KEGG pathways, and Gene Ontology Biological Processes of level 3.
source: To reduce redundancy and facilitate the understanding of their biological relevance, we clustered those pathways into families that also include Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways (Kanehisa and Goto, 2000) and Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Processes of level 3 (Gene Ontology Consortium, 2004).
evidence: The Results section describes the pathway clustering approach with citations.

claim: There is an overlap of pathways related to metabolism in the two peaks of altered genes in subcutaneous adipose tissue.
source: For example, although most pathways enriched in the two aforementioned peaks of altered genes in subcutaneous adipose tissue were different, there is an overlap of pathways related to metabolism, including various mitochondrial processes (Figure 4A).
evidence: The Results section describes this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: voyAGEr enables the user to visualise how the expression of modules of genes that are associated with a specific cell type, biological pathway, or disease progresses over age in a specific tissue.
source: Concretely, voyAGEr enables the user to visualise how the expression of modules of genes that are associated with a specific cell type, biological pathway, or disease progresses over age in a specific tissue.
evidence: The Results section describes this functionality.

claim: The 'MEblue' module in brain cortex shows significant enrichment in astrocyte markers.
source: In the example of Figure 5C, the 'MEblue' module, comprising 241 genes co-expressed in the brain cortex, shows significant enrichment in astrocyte markers.
evidence: The Results section describes this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The apparent increase of the 'MEblue' module's expression with age may reflect the known age-related changes in astrocyte activation.
source: The apparent increase of this module's expression with age may reflect the known age-related changes in astrocyte activation (Palmer and Ousman, 2018) and the relative weakening of neuronal activity ('MEyellow' and 'MEpink' modules).
evidence: The Results section interprets the finding with a citation.

claim: voyAGEr provides a framework to examine the progression of gene expression over age in several human tissues.
source: voyAGEr provides a framework to examine the progression of gene expression over age in several human tissues, serving as a valuable resource for the ageing research community.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the tool's purpose.

claim: The results show the complexity of human biological ageing by stressing its tissue specificity and non-linear transcriptional progression throughout the lifetime.
source: The results of our analyses show the complexity of human biological ageing by stressing its tissue specificity (Gheorghe et al., 2014) and non-linear transcriptional progression throughout the lifetime, consistent with previous results from both proteomic (Lehallier et al., 2019) and transcriptomic (Haustead et al., 2016; Gheorghe et al., 2014) analyses.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes findings with citations.

claim: voyAGEr may not be always suited for direct comparisons between different tissues.
source: Due to the tissue-specific nature of the pre-processing steps (v. Read count data pre-processing in the Methods section), and given that most of the plotted gene expression distributions are centered and scaled by tissue, it is important to note that voyAGEr may not be always suited for direct comparisons between different tissues.
evidence: The Discussion section identifies this limitation.

claim: The majority of GTEx donors contributed samples to multiple tissues.
source: Furthermore, we must emphasise that the majority of GTEx donors contributed samples to multiple tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 ), potentially introducing biases and confounders when comparing gene expression patterns between tissues.
evidence: The Discussion section identifies this potential confounding factor.

claim: Analyses of variance and downsampling to control for common donors suggest very limited global confounding between the impacts of donor and age on gene expression.
source: Our analyses of variance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B ) and downsampling to control for common donors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E) suggest very limited global confounding between the impacts of donor and age on gene expression and that any potential cross-tissue bias not to depend much on the proportion of common donors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The Discussion section describes analyses addressing potential confounding.

claim: Biological sex is an important factor in the prevalence of ageing-associated diseases, as well as their age of onset and progression.
source: Biological sex is an important factor in the prevalence of ageing-associated diseases, as well as their age of onset, progression (Tower, 2017; Austad and Fischer, 2016; Khramtsova et al., 2019), and sex-related differences in gene expression (Melé et al., 2015; Gershoni and Pietrokovski, 2017; Kassam et al., 2019; Mayne et al., 2016).
evidence: The Discussion section cites published literature supporting this claim.

claim: voyAGEr was able to corroborate findings on the sex-differential transcriptome of adult humans by Gershoni and Pietrokovski, 2017.
source: For instance, we were able to corroborate findings on the sex-differential transcriptome of adult humans by Gershoni and Pietrokovski, 2017, with voyAGEr emphasising its tissue-specificity and allowing to discriminate the ages at which sex-related biases appear to be more prevalent (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Discussion section describes validation of previous findings.

claim: It is essential to interpret sex chromosome-specific gene results in voyAGEr with caution.
source: Nonetheless, it is essential to interpret sex chromosome-specific gene results in voyAGEr with caution.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a cautionary note.

claim: Most GTEx tissue donors had health conditions and their frequency increased with age.
source: One of the limitations of voyAGEr is that most GTEx tissue donors had health conditions and their frequency increased with age, preventing us from defining a class of healthy individuals and identifying age-associated transcriptomic changes that could be more confidently proposed to happen independently of any disease progression.
evidence: The Discussion section identifies this limitation.

claim: The large sample sizes and inherent biological variability among individuals are expected to mitigate significant confounding effects from health conditions.
source: Whilst the large sample sizes and inherent biological variability among individuals, reflected in the diversity of condition combinations, are expected to mitigate significant confounding effects, voyAGEr also allows users to evaluate how tissue-specific gene expression trends vary according to the donors' diverse conditions (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The Discussion section addresses this limitation with reasoning.

claim: ShARP-LM facilitates the holistic depiction of the transcriptional landscapes of adult human tissues throughout ageing with a yearly age resolution.
source: The development of voyAGEr was accompanied by that of a pipeline, ShARP-LM, that facilitates the holistic depiction of the transcriptional landscapes of adult human tissues throughout ageing with a yearly age resolution.
evidence: The Discussion section describes the pipeline's capabilities.

claim: The age distribution of donors impacts the statistical power for detecting transcriptional changes.
source: Nevertheless, it is worth highlighting that the age distribution of donors does impact the statistical power for detecting transcriptional changes. Consequently, we are more likely to identify significant alterations (with p-value <0.05 in our gene-centric analyses) within age ranges that are more prevalent in our sample population, often characterised by older individuals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Discussion section identifies this limitation.

claim: When downsampling to ensure a balanced age distribution, a loss of statistical power is apparent but a considerable positive correlation with the original results is maintained.
source: When downsampling to ensure a balanced age distribution, a loss of statistical power is apparent but a considerable positive correlation with the original results is maintained and a substantial number of significant alterations remain so (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The Discussion section describes downsampling analysis results.

claim: The accumulation of transcriptomes of human tissues in public databases promises a gradual increase in accuracy and age resolution with which human transcriptomic ageing can be profiled.
source: This limitation is likely to be overcome by the accumulation of transcriptomes of human tissues in public databases, promising a gradual increase in accuracy and age resolution with which human transcriptomic ageing can be profiled.
evidence: The Discussion section speculates on future improvements.

claim: It is imperative to approach the module-based analysis with caution, as direct and literal interpretations may be misleading.
source: Nonetheless, it is imperative to approach the module-based analysis with caution, as direct and literal interpretations may be misleading.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a cautionary note.

claim: voyAGEr is envisaged to be a continually evolving resource, able to accommodate new data and expand its functionalities.
source: Given its open-source nature, voyAGEr is envisaged to be a continually evolving resource, able to accommodate new data and expand its functionalities, namely by incorporating additional tissues into the modules section and integrating perturbagen data for inference of molecular causes underlying observed gene expression alterations and small molecules to target them for therapeutic purposes (Subramanian et al., 2017; Saraiva-Agostinho and de Almeida, 2020).
evidence: The Discussion section describes future plans with citations.

claim: voyAGEr is meant to be a discovery tool, supporting biologists in the exploration of a large transcriptomic dataset.
source: As an in silico approach with no experimental validation for its results, voyAGEr is meant to be a discovery tool, supporting biologists in the exploration of a large transcriptomic dataset, thereby generating, refining, or preliminary testing hypotheses, laying the groundwork for subsequent experimental research.
evidence: The Discussion section describes the tool's intended use.

claim: The observed diverse and asynchronous changes in gene expression between tissues over the human adult life provide potentially relevant information for the design of accurate diagnostic tools and personalised therapies.
source: Moreover, the observed diverse and asynchronous changes in gene expression between tissues over the human adult life provide potentially relevant information for the design of accurate diagnostic tools and personalised therapies.
evidence: The Discussion section speculates on potential applications.

claim: Data analysis was performed in R (version 4.1.2).
source: Data analysis was performed in R (version 4.1.2) and the application developed with R package Shiny (Chang et al., 2024).
evidence: The Methods section specifies the software used.

claim: The application was developed with R package Shiny.
source: Data analysis was performed in R (version 4.1.2) and the application developed with R package Shiny (Chang et al., 2024).
evidence: The Methods section specifies the software used with citation.

claim: voyAGEr was deployed using Docker Compose and ShinyProxy 2.6.1.
source: voyAGEr was deployed using Docker Compose and ShinyProxy 2.6.1 in a Linux virtual machine (64 GB RAM, 16 CPU threads, and 200 GB SSD) running in our institutional computing cluster.
evidence: The Methods section specifies the deployment infrastructure.

claim: The matrix with the RNA-seq read counts for each gene in each GTEx v8 sample was downloaded from the project's data portal.
source: The matrix with the RNA-seq read counts for each gene in each GTEx v8 sample was downloaded from the project's data portal (https://www.gtexportal.org/) (Lonsdale et al., 2013).
evidence: The Methods section describes the data source with citation.

claim: Five tissues were discarded (kidney medulla, fallopian tube, bladder, ectocervix, endocervix) due to low (<50) numbers of samples.
source: From the 54 tissues available from GTEx v8, five were discarded (kidney medulla, fallopian tube, bladder, ectocervix, endocervix) due to low (<50) numbers of samples.
evidence: The Methods section describes data filtering criteria.

claim: Only genes with at least one CPM in at least 40% of the samples were kept for analysis.
source: We started by filtering out genes deemed uninformative due to their very low expression across samples: only genes with at least one CPM in at least 40% of the samples were kept for analysis (the number of genes analysed for each tissue can be found in Supplementary file 1; Robinson et al., 2010).
evidence: The Methods section describes gene filtering criteria with citation.

claim: Read counts were normalised and log-transformed with the voom function from package limma.
source: Read counts were subsequently normalised and log-transformed with the voom function (Law et al., 2014) from package limma (Ritchie et al., 2015).
evidence: The Methods section describes normalization procedure with citations.

claim: Batch effects can introduce spurious gene expression differences between samples and result in confounding factors.
source: However, it is well-established that batch effects, which may stem from variations in sample treatment prior to RNA-seq library preparation, can introduce spurious gene expression differences between samples and result in confounding factors (García-Pérez et al., 2023).
evidence: The Methods section cites published literature on batch effects.

claim: The COHORT variable appeared to be the main batch effect in most tissues except brain tissues.
source: Except in brain tissues, the COHORT variable (i.e. whether the samples were collected from organ donors or post-mortem) appeared to be the main batch effect, with ripple effects on numerous other related conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Methods section describes batch effect analysis results.

claim: SMRIN, DTHHRDY, and MHSMKYRS consistently emerged as conditions associated with the primary axes of variance.
source: Moreover, SMRIN (sample's RNA integrity number), DTHHRDY (death classification based on the 4-point Hardy Scale), and MHSMKYRS (smoke years) consistently emerged as conditions associated with the primary axes of variance.
evidence: The Methods section describes variance analysis results.

claim: Batch correction was performed for five conditions: COHORT, SMRIN, DTHHRDY, MHSMKYRS, and the number of genes detected in each sample.
source: We, therefore, corrected for these five conditions, on a tissue-by-tissue basis, by adapting the removeBatchEffect function from the limma package (Ritchie et al., 2015).
evidence: The Methods section describes batch correction procedure with citation.

claim: Imputation was carried out using the mice package to prevent sample loss due to missing values.
source: To prevent sample loss due to missing values for the aforementioned five conditions and since the number of missing values was relatively low compared to the total number of samples, imputation was carried out using the mice package (Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011).
evidence: The Methods section describes imputation procedure with citation.

claim: Without batch correction, SFTPA2 expression would have been associated with age due to the higher prevalence of ventilator cases among older individuals.
source: As an illustrative example of the importance of batch removal, the expression of surfactant factor SFTPA2 was found to be associated with donors on a ventilator (McCall et al., 2016). Without batch correction, SFTPA2 expression would have been associated with age due to the higher prevalence of such cases among older individuals (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The Methods section provides an example of batch effect impact with citation.

claim: The trend of each gene's expression progression over age in each tissue was derived through Local Polynomial Regression Fitting using R function loess.
source: For visualisation purposes, the trend of each gene's expression progression over age in each tissue was derived through Local Polynomial Regression Fitting, using R function loess on logCPM values (Figures 1—3).
evidence: The Methods section describes visualization methodology.

claim: FDR was controlled by randomly permuting the samples' ages and sexes within each age window fifty thousand times.
source: To evaluate the significance of each percentage and assess if high percentages can be confidently associated with major transcriptomic alterations, we controlled for their false discovery rate (FDR) by randomly permuting the samples' ages and sexes within each age window fifty thousand times and performing ShARP-LM on each randomised dataset.
evidence: The Methods section describes FDR control procedure.

claim: GSEA was performed using R package fgsea and the Reactome database.
source: For each Peak of significant gene expression modifications, we performed GSEA (Subramanian et al., 2005) on the ordered (from the most positive to the most negative) t-statistics of differential expression for the respective tissue and age, using R package fgsea (Korotkevich et al., 2021) and the Reactome database (Croft et al., 2014).
evidence: The Methods section describes GSEA procedure with citations.

claim: Only pathways containing a minimum of 15 genes and up to 500 genes were considered.
source: To optimise computational efficiency and minimise redundancy in the analysed pathways, we only considered pathways containing a minimum of 15 genes and up to 500 genes, as suggested in the GSEA User Guide (GSEA-MSIGDB, 2023).
evidence: The Methods section describes pathway filtering criteria with citation.

claim: Gene co-expression modules were defined with R package WGCNA.
source: Gene co-expression modules were defined with R package WGCNA (Langfelder and Horvath, 2008).
evidence: The Methods section describes module definition methodology with citation.

claim: The value of β=12 was chosen for soft thresholding in accordance with the WGCNA FAQs.
source: We then applied soft thresholding by raising all correlation values to the power of β, accentuating stronger correlations. The value of β=12 was chosen in accordance with the WGCNA FAQs (Langfelder and Horvath, 2024), and after confirmation of a free-scale topology using the pickSoftThreshold function.
evidence: The Methods section describes parameter selection with citation.

claim: Cell type enrichment analysis relied on Fisher tests.
source: Cell-type enrichment analysis relied on Fisher tests, providing odds enrichment scores and significance values (p-values).
evidence: The Methods section describes enrichment analysis methodology.

claim: Cell type signatures were sourced from MSigDB's C8 collection.
source: The cell type signatures employed in this analysis were sourced from MSigDB's C8 collection (Subramanian et al., 2005), and in the case of Whole Blood, additionally from LM22 (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: The Methods section describes data sources with citations.

claim: The four tissues covered by the Module section were selected due to their relatively high sample sizes and availability of comprehensive cell type signatures.
source: The four tissues (Brain - Cortex, Muscle - Skeletal, Heart - Left Ventricle, and Whole Blood) covered by the Module section of voyAGEr were selected due to their relatively high sample sizes and availability of comprehensive cell type signatures.
